Differences in Skilled Nursing Facilities Admitting Medicare Patients With and Without COVID‑19 After Hospitalization

J Gen Intern Med 41(1):232–5 DOI: 10.1007/s11606-025-09667-4 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Society of General Internal Medicine 2025

# INTRODUCTION

During the COVID-19 pandemic, a major challenge was efficiently discharging stabilized hospital patients with COVID- 19 to maintain acute care capacity during regional infection surges. Skilled nursing facilities (SNFs), which play a critical role in post-acute care, hesitated to admit COVID-19 patients due to the vulnerability of their long-term residents. In response, states implemented policies to encourage SNFs to accept COVID-19 patients, including providing financial incentives.1 Despite such efforts, the proportion of SNFs receiving COVID-19 patients remained low and fluctuated around 10%.2 Given the two-tiered system where higher star-rated SNFs are generally better equipped to deliver post-acute ­care3, it remains unclear which types of SNFs admitted COVID-19 patients. This study addresses this gap by comparing the CMS-reported star ratings of SNFs that admitted hospital patients with and without COVID-19.

## METHODS

We used Medicare claims and the Minimum Data Set to identify post-acute SNF admissions and assessed differences in characteristics of SNFs admitting COVID-19 and non- COVID-19 patients. We identified all SNF admissions from January 2018 to December 2021 for Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 years and older who were admitted to a SNF within 1 day after hospital discharge. We excluded patients who had a hospital or SNF stay 6 months prior to their index hospitalization to minimize the influence of recent health care use on discharge locations. Previous studies assessing postacute care outcomes adopted similar exclusion criteria.4,5 We classified SNF admissions as COVID-19 admissions using patient’s index hospital claims following the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) method (admissions before the pandemic were coded as non-COVID-19). 6 We used March 1, 2020, as the start date of the pandemic. Patient demographics including age, sex, race and ethnicity, dual eligibility for Medicare and Medicaid, and enrollment

in traditional Medicare, comorbidities, hospital length of stays, and admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) were identified using Medicare data. Primary outcomes include binary indicators for pre-pandemic four or five stars in overall, survey, staffing, or shortstay quality measure ratings, which are publicly reported by CMS and are related to patient health outcomes.7 We also examined distances to the admitting SNF from discharging hospitals and from patients’ home ZIP Codes as secondary outcomes. We used a separate linear regression model for each outcome to estimate differences between COVID-19 and non- COVID-19 admissions. The explanatory variables include calendar month-year indicators, the patient’s COVID-19 status, interactions between the month-year and COVID-19 indicators, beneficiary demographics, clinical characteristics, and fixed effects for both hospital and beneficiary ZIP Codes.

## RESULTS

We identified 3,346,741 SNF admissions for non-COVID-19 patients and 112,340 admissions for COVID-19 patients (Table 1). Compared to newly admitted patients without COVID-19, COVID-19 patients were more likely to be dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid (28.5% vs 22.4%) and more likely to be admitted to ICUs during hospitalizations (37.8% vs 31.4%). Adjusted likelihoods of discharge to high-rating facilities for non-COVID-19 patients were similar before and during the pandemic (Fig. 1). However, COVID-19 admissions were less likely than non-COVID-19 admissions to be discharged to a high-quality SNF. They were 9.79 percentage points (95% CI, − 10.66, − 8.93) less likely to be discharged to a 4- or 5-star overall-rated SNF, 7.31 percentage points (95% CI − 8.20, − 6.41) less likely to a 4- or 5-star survey-rated facility, 6.33 percentage points (95% CI − 7.13, − 5.54) less likely to a 4- or 5-star staffing-rated facility, and 4.70 percentage points (95% CI, − 5.48, − 3.91) less likely to a 4- or 5-star short-stay quality measure-rated facility. Compared to non-COVID-19 admissions, COVID- 19 admissions were discharged to SNFs farther away from the discharging hospital and from the beneficiary’s home ZIP code.

## DISCUSSION

These results show that COVID-19 Medicare patients were admitted to SNFs of lower quality across multiple dimensions and had to travel farther distances to receive SNF care than non-COVID-19 patients. Medicare COVID-19 hospital patients faced limited options for post-acute SNF care, indicating disparities in care transitions for vulnerable populations. Future study should identify factors that impacted nursing homes’ admission decisions during the pandemic, which are critical for policymakers to design better strategies

to ensure access to lower-level care for infectious disease patients. Limitations of the study include potential misclassification of COVID-19 diagnosis in Medicare claims data, the lack of generalizability to other populations, and unmeasured residual confounding.

*Figure 1   Characteristics of admitting skilled nursing facilities (SNF) by COVID-19 diagnosis. Subtitle: Adjusted trends with 95% confidence interval (CI), 2018–2021. Blue, non-COVID admission; pink, COVID admission. We used March 1, 2020, as the start date of the COVID-19 pandemic. A SNF admission was defined as COVID-19 admission if the beneficiary had one of the following ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes documented on their Medicare Provider Analysis and Review (MedPAR) files: U07.1 and B97.29. If not, the admission was defined as non-COVID-19 admission. The Medicare overall star rating (ranging from 1, poor, to 5, excellent), survey star rating, staff star rating, and short-stay quality measure rating were obtained from the Nursing Home Compare website. For each SNF, we defined their ratings as the maximum mode value of all their star ratings between 2018 and 2019. A binary indicator for whether the rating achieved 4 or 5 stars was then created as the primary SNF characteristic. Ellipsoidal distances were calculated using coordinates of each location, which were obtained from CASPER data for a SNF, from AHA annual survey data for a hospital, and from the SAS ZIP Code data file for a ZIP code centroid. For each SNF characteristic, we fit a linear regression model with calendar month-year indicators, the COVID-19 indicator, and interactions between each month-year and the COVID-19 indicators, adjusting for beneficiary demographics and clinical conditions, as well as hospital and beneficiary ZIP code fixed effects. Standard errors were clustered at the hospital level. Adjusted likelihoods of admitting to 4- or 5-star facilities and their 95% confidence intervals were calculated for COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 admissions at each calendar month-year using fitted values from the regression and taking all other variables as is except for the COVID-19 indicator and month-year indicator. Overall adjusted differences were estimated in a similar way by keeping all variables as is except for the COVID-19 indicator.*
